title: Putting it together
summary: Combine everything you've learned into one polished, end-to-end portfolio project that proves you can ship real AI work.
objectives: Scope a focused project that tells a clear story to recruiters
Wire data, an LLM call, and an interface into one working app
Keep API keys and secrets out of your code with environment variables
Write a README that lets anyone run your project in minutes
Add basic tests and error handling so the demo doesn't break
Deploy or record a demo so the project is easy to view
Present the project with results, trade-offs, and next steps

quiz.q: What is the best way to store your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in a portfolio project?
options: Paste it directly in the code
In an environment variable, read with os.environ
In the README so reviewers can use it
In a public config.json committed to GitHub
quiz.why: Secrets belong in environment variables (or a .env file that is git-ignored), never hard-coded or committed where others can see them.

quiz.q: Which file makes a portfolio project easy for a stranger to run?
options: All of these help, but the README is the entry point
quiz.why: A clear README explains what the project does and how to run it; requirements.txt and LICENSE support it, but the README is what a recruiter reads first.

quiz.q: Why scope a portfolio project narrowly rather than building something huge?
options: A finished, focused project beats an impressive unfinished one
quiz.why: One small project you actually finished and can demo cleanly is far more convincing than a sprawling one that doesn't run.

quiz.q: Name one thing your README should always include so someone can run your project.
quiz.answer: Setup/install and run instructions (e.g. install dependencies, set the API key, run the command).
quiz.why: Without clear setup and run steps, even great code is useless to a reviewer who can't get it started.

quiz.q: In one phrase, what should the final slide of a project presentation cover?
quiz.answer: Results, trade-offs you made, and what you would do next.
quiz.why: Closing with results and honest next steps shows engineering judgement, which is what employers are really assessing.

quiz.q: What does pinning versions in requirements.txt (e.g. anthropic==0.39.0) protect against?
options: A future package update silently breaking your app
quiz.why: Pinned versions make the project reproducible: it installs the same dependencies today and months from now, so it keeps working.

body_markdown:
## The goal: one project that proves it

After four months you can write Python, use Git, query data, and call an LLM. This lesson is about **putting it together** into a single portfolio project a recruiter can open, understand, and run.

The aim is not size — it's a **finished, focused** project that tells a clear story: *here is a real problem, here is how I used AI to solve it, here is the result.*

## Scope it small, ship it whole

Pick one narrow problem. A good shape is: take some **input**, send it to **Claude**, return a useful **output**, wrapped in a small interface.

Examples that work well: a CV-to-cover-letter helper, a support-ticket classifier, a notes summariser. Each is small enough to finish and clear enough to explain.

Write down, in one sentence, what done looks like. Then build to that and stop.

## The core: data in, Claude in the middle, result out

Here is the heart of almost every project — a clean call to the Claude Messages API. Keep your key in an environment variable, never in the code.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

def summarise(text: str) -> str:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarise in 3 bullets:\n{text}"}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text
```

## Make it runnable by a stranger

A project a reviewer can't run might as well not exist. Pin your dependencies and set the key from the shell.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # Windows: set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
streamlit run app.py
```

Your `requirements.txt` should pin versions, for example `anthropic==0.39.0` and `streamlit==1.39.0`, so it installs the same way every time.

## Polish: README, tests, and a demo

Three things turn code into a portfolio piece:

- **README** — one-line description, a screenshot, setup steps, and how to run it.
- **A test or two** — even one `assert` that your function returns text proves you think about correctness.
- **A demo** — deploy it or record a 60-second screen capture, and link it at the top of the README.

Add simple error handling so a missing key or empty input shows a friendly message instead of a stack trace.

## Present it like an engineer

When you talk about the project, cover three things: **the result**, the **trade-offs** you made (why this model, why this scope), and **what you'd do next**. That honesty is exactly the judgement employers are hiring for.

## Your task

Ship one end-to-end project this week: scope it in a sentence, build the data-to-Claude-to-output core, write the README, and record a short demo.

slides.title: Putting it together
slides.narration: Welcome to the lesson where it all comes together. Over four months you've learned Python, Git, working with data, and calling an A I model. Today we put those pieces into one finished portfolio project, the kind a recruiter can open, understand, and run. The goal isn't to build something huge. It's to ship something whole.

slides.title: Why one project matters
bullets: A finished project beats an impressive unfinished one.
It tells a story: problem, AI solution, result.
Recruiters want proof you can ship.
slides.narration: Let's start with why this matters so much. One small project you actually finished, and can demo cleanly, is far more convincing than a sprawling idea that doesn't run. A good portfolio piece tells a story. Here's a real problem, here's how I used A I to solve it, and here's the result. That's what proves you can ship.

slides.title: Scope it small
bullets: Pick one narrow problem.
Input goes in, Claude responds, output comes out.
Write one sentence describing done — then stop.
slides.narration: The biggest mistake beginners make is scoping too big. Pick one narrow problem. A great shape is simple: some input goes in, Claude in the middle does the thinking, and a useful output comes out. Before you write any code, write one sentence describing what done looks like. Then build exactly to that, and stop.

slides.title: Good project ideas
bullets: CV to cover-letter helper.
Support-ticket classifier.
Notes or document summariser.
slides.narration: Here are three ideas that work beautifully. A C V to cover-letter helper. A support-ticket classifier, which is perfect given your L one support background. Or a notes summariser. Each one is small enough to finish in a week, and clear enough that you can explain it in a single sentence at interview.

slides.title: The core call
bullets: Read the key from an environment variable.
Send input to the Claude Messages API.
Return the model's text response.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role":"user","content":text}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Here's the heart of almost every project: a clean call to the Claude Messages A P I. We create a client, which automatically reads your A P I key from the environment. We call messages dot create, passing a model, a max tokens limit, and a list of messages. The model's reply comes back in msg dot content, and we grab the text. That's the whole engine.

slides.title: Keep secrets safe
bullets: Never paste your API key in the code.
Use an environment variable or a git-ignored .env.
Never commit secrets to GitHub.
slides.narration: This one is critical. Never paste your A P I key directly into your code, and never commit it to GitHub. Instead, set it as an environment variable, like you see here, or keep it in a dot env file that you add to git ignore. The Anthropic client picks it up automatically. Leaking a key is one of the fastest ways to look unprofessional, so build the safe habit now.

slides.title: Make it runnable
bullets: Pin versions in requirements.txt.
Document setup and run steps.
A stranger should run it in minutes.
slides.code:
python -m venv .venv
pip install -r requirements.txt
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
streamlit run app.py
slides.narration: A project a reviewer can't run might as well not exist. So pin your dependency versions in requirements dot t x t, so it installs the same way every time. Then document the exact steps: create a virtual environment, install, set the key, and run. The test is simple. Could a stranger clone your repo and have it running in a few minutes?

slides.title: Polish that pays off
bullets: README: description, screenshot, how to run.
One or two small tests.
A deployed link or 60-second demo video.
slides.narration: Three things turn code into a portfolio piece. First, a README with a one-line description, a screenshot, and clear run steps. Second, even one or two small tests, which show you think about correctness. And third, a demo. Either deploy it, or record a sixty second screen capture and link it right at the top of your README. Reviewers love being able to see it work instantly.

slides.title: Handle errors gracefully
bullets: Catch a missing key or empty input.
Show a friendly message, not a crash.
A robust demo earns trust.
slides.narration: Nothing kills a live demo like a stack trace. So add simple guards. Check for empty input before you call the model. Wrap the A P I call in a try except so a missing key or a network hiccup shows a friendly message instead of crashing. It's a tiny amount of code, but it makes your project feel solid and trustworthy.

slides.title: Present like an engineer
bullets: Show the result clearly.
Explain your trade-offs and choices.
Say what you'd do next.
slides.narration: When you talk about your project, cover three things. The result, shown clearly. The trade-offs you made, like why you chose this model and this scope. And what you'd do next if you had more time. That honesty about choices and limits is exactly the engineering judgement that employers are really hiring for.

Data to Claude to output is the core.
Keep keys in env vars; pin dependencies.
README, tests, and a demo sell it.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Scope your project small and ship it whole. The core is always data going in, Claude in the middle, output coming out. Keep your keys in environment variables and pin your dependencies. Then a README, a test or two, and a demo turn it into a portfolio piece.
